content: Human papillomavirus (HPV) is a diverse group of DNA-based viruses that infect the skin and mucous membranes of humans and various animals. Over 100 different types of HPV have been identified. Certain HPV types can cause skin warts (condylomas), while others may lead to subclinical infections that result in precancerous lesions. All HPV types are transmitted through skin-to-skin contact. A subset of 30-40 HPV types is typically transmitted via sexual contact, infecting the anogenital region. Among these, types 6 and 11 are known to cause genital warts, while other types may infect the genital area without causing noticeable symptoms. Persistent infection with approximately 13 high-risk sexually transmitted HPV types, including types 16, 18, 31, 33, 35, 39, 45, 51, 52, 56, 58, 59, and 68, can lead to the development of precancerous lesions such as cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN), vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia (VIN), penile intraepithelial neoplasia (PIN), and anal intraepithelial neoplasia (AIN). These lesions have the potential to progress to invasive cancer. HPV infection is a necessary factor in the development of nearly all cases of cervical cancer. Historically, researchers observed that cervical cancer rates were significantly higher in prostitutes compared to nuns, leading to the hypothesis of a causal link between sexually transmitted HPVs and cervical cancer. HPV is classified based on the anatomical region it affects and the specific virus type. It is primarily divided into cutaneous, anogenital, and other mucosal surface types. To date, 210 different HPV types have been discovered, and this number continues to grow. The clinical manifestations of HPV infection depend on the virus type and the anatomical area involved. HPV is most commonly transmitted through sexual contact. The virus's life cycle is closely linked to the differentiation and maturation of host epithelial cells, with specific gene products being transcribed at various stages. The oncogenic potential of HPV, particularly high-risk types (16, 18, 31, 33, 35, 39, 45, 51, 52, 56, 58, 59, and 68), is mediated by the viral proteins E6 and E7. These proteins interact with critical host cell cycle regulatory proteins, p53 and Rb, leading to unchecked cellular replication, accumulation of mutations, and ultimately cancer development. Genital HPV infection is highly prevalent, with estimates suggesting that more than 50% of women will acquire one or more sexually transmitted HPV types during adulthood. Risk factors for anogenital HPV infection include a high number of sexual partners, having a new partner, prolonged sexual activity, vaginal delivery, and multiple deliveries. Close contact is the most significant risk factor for cutaneous HPV infection. High-risk HPV types are associated with 70% of cervical cancers in women with persistent infections. Due to this strong association, cervical cancer screening is recommended for all women starting at age 21. The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) advises screening women aged 21 to 65 for cervical cancer. Most HPV infections are subclinical, asymptomatic, and resolve without complications in immunocompetent individuals. The time to symptom development varies: genital warts may appear within 3 weeks to 3 months, cellular abnormalities (metaplasia and dysplasia) may take months to years, and cancers may take several years to develop. Persistent HPV infection is associated with risk factors such as multiple sexual partners, alcohol consumption, immunosuppression, older age, and prior detection of multiple HPV types. Without treatment, low-risk HPV types may resolve spontaneously or persist as warty lesions. The prognosis of HPV infection depends on the specific HPV type involved. A detailed sexual history and physical examination are essential for patients with anogenital involvement. Symptoms are often related to skin irritation and mucosal surface involvement. While pruritus is a hallmark of cutaneous involvement, most individuals with HPV are asymptomatic. The clinical manifestation of HPV infection is often warts, which may sometimes be painful. Certain sexually transmitted HPV types are strongly associated with cervical cancer. Persistent infection with high-risk HPV types is a critical factor in nearly all cases of cervical cancer. The progression from HPV infection to cervical cancer is a slow process, often taking years. During this time, precancerous cells can be detected through regular cervical cytology (Pap smear) screening. A Pap smear combined with HPV DNA testing can identify cellular abnormalities and the presence of HPV, enabling targeted surgical removal of condylomatous or precancerous lesions before invasive cervical cancer develops. While widespread Pap testing has reduced cervical cancer incidence and mortality in developed countries, the disease still claims hundreds of thousands of lives annually worldwide. The recently approved HPV vaccine, Gardasil, which prevents initial infection with several common sexually transmitted HPV types, may further reduce the incidence of HPV-induced cancers. There is no definitive medical treatment for HPV infection. Treatment primarily focuses on managing warts or precancerous lesions. Two main therapeutic approaches are cytodestructive therapy and immunotherapy, with no single treatment considered superior. Treatment selection depends on factors such as wart size, number, anatomical site, morphology, patient preference, cost, convenience, and potential adverse effects. Medical therapies for HPV infection include imiquimod, sinecatechins, or podofilox. Surgical removal of external genital warts is an alternative to pharmacologic therapy and may involve tangential scissor excision, tangential shave excision, curettage, laser therapy, or electrosurgery. Most individuals acquire various cutaneous HPV types during childhood. The virus's robust outer protein shell, or capsid, allows it to persist in the environment for extended periods. Avoiding contact with contaminated surfaces, such as communal shower floors or airport security lines, may reduce the risk of cutaneous HPV infection. Treating common warts promptly after they appear may also limit the spread of infection to additional sites. Genital HPV infections can be widely distributed across genital skin and mucosal surfaces, and transmission can occur even in the absence of overt symptoms.
